items.title: Fundamental Rights — Part III Overview
items.body:
## In one line

Fundamental Rights (FR), in Part III, Articles 12-35, are the basic freedoms the Constitution guarantees and that courts can directly enforce.

## Why it is asked

The structure of Part III and the FR-versus-DPSP (enforceable against non-enforceable) contrast anchor many questions.

## What & Where

- **Fundamental Rights (FRs)** are guaranteed in **Part III (Articles 12-35)** of the Constitution. They were inspired by the **US Bill of Rights** and the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)**.
- Often called the **Magna Carta of India**, they limit the power of the State and are **justiciable** — enforceable in court.

## Articles 12 and 13 — who is bound, and what happens to a law that breaks an FR

- **Article 12** defines **'the State'** against which FRs can be claimed. It includes: (1) the **Government and Parliament of India**; (2) the **Government and Legislature of each State**; (3) all **local authorities** such as **municipalities and panchayats**; and (4) **other authorities within the territory of India** or under the control of the Government of India (for example, statutory bodies such as LIC or ONGC).
- **Article 13** declares that any law **inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights shall be void** to the extent of the inconsistency. This is the basis of **judicial review** of laws for FR violations.

**Don't confuse:** the **right to vote and to be elected** is NOT a Fundamental Right. Voting rests on **universal adult franchise (Article 326)** and the election laws, so it is a **constitutional/legal right**, not part of Part III.

## Six Rights (originally seven)

| Right | Articles |
|---|---|
| Right to Equality | 14-18 |
| Right to Freedom | 19-22 |
| Right against Exploitation | 23-24 |
| Right to Freedom of Religion | 25-28 |
| Cultural & Educational Rights | 29-30 |
| Right to Constitutional Remedies | 32 |

- The **Right to Property** (old Art 19(1)(f) & 31) was the **seventh** right; the **44th Amendment Act, 1978** deleted it from Part III and made it an ordinary **legal/constitutional right under Article 300A** (Part XII).
- FRs are **not absolute** — the State may impose **reasonable restrictions** (public order, morality, sovereignty, etc.).
- Some FRs are for **citizens only** (Arts 15, 16, 19, 29, 30); others (Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25-28) apply to **all persons**, including foreigners.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Fundamental Rights (Part III) | Directive Principles (Part IV) |
|---|---|---|
| Enforceable in court? | Yes (justiciable) | No (non-justiciable) |
| Addressed to | The State; some rights to all persons | The State only |
| Nature | Mostly negative — they limit State power | Positive — goals the State should pursue |

## Terms explained

- **Fundamental Rights (FR)** — basic freedoms in Part III that a person can directly ask a court to enforce.
- **Justiciable** — enforceable in a court of law.
- **Reasonable restrictions** — lawful limits the State may place on a right (for public order, morality and so on).
- **Magna Carta** — a famous historic charter of rights, used here as a nickname for Part III.

## TL;DR

- Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12-35, inspired by the US Bill of Rights and UDHR.
- There are now six FRs; the Right to Property was removed by the 44th Amendment 1978 and made a legal right under Article 300A.
- Right to Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Cultural-Educational (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32).
- FRs are justiciable but not absolute — subject to reasonable restrictions.
- Arts 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 are for citizens only; Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 25-28 apply to all persons.
keyPoints: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12-35, inspired by the US Bill of Rights and UDHR.
There are now six FRs; the Right to Property was removed by the 44th Amendment 1978 and made a legal right under Article 300A.
Right to Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Cultural-Educational (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32).

Article 12 'State' = Union Government and Parliament, State Governments and Legislatures, local authorities (municipalities, panchayats) and other authorities; Article 13 voids laws that violate FRs (basis of judicial review).
The right to vote and to be elected is a constitutional/legal right (Art 326), not a Fundamental Right.

items.title: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)
items.body:
## In one line

Articles 14-18 guarantee equality before the law and ban discrimination, untouchability and titles.

## Why it is asked

Reservation clauses (15(3), 15(4), 16(4)) and the untouchability article are heavily tested.

## Article 14 — Equality

- Guarantees **equality before law** (British concept — no one above the law) and **equal protection of the laws** (American concept — like treated alike). Applies to **all persons**.
- Article 14 also embodies the **Rule of Law** and bars **arbitrariness**: a law that gives the executive **unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power** in applying it can be struck down for violating Article 14.

## Articles 15-18

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 15 | Prohibits discrimination on **religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth**; **15(3)** allows special provisions for women & children; **15(4)** for the advancement of **socially and educationally backward classes** and SC/ST |
| 16 | **Equality of opportunity** in public employment; **16(4)** permits **reservation of appointments** for backward classes **not adequately represented** in State services |
| 17 | **Abolition of untouchability**; its practice is an offence (Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955) |
| 18 | **Abolition of titles** — bars State titles; **military and academic** distinctions are exempt; **Bharat Ratna/Padma awards are not titles** |

- Articles **15, 16** are available to **citizens only**; Articles **14, 17, 18** apply to all.

## Terms explained

- **Equality before law** — the British idea that no one is above the law.
- **Equal protection of the laws** — the American idea that people in like situations must be treated alike.
- **Reservation** — a reserved share of seats or jobs for backward classes.
- **Untouchability** — the social practice of treating certain castes as impure, abolished by Article 17.

## TL;DR

- Article 14 = equality before law (British) + equal protection of laws (American); applies to all persons.
- Article 15 bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; 15(3) favours women/children, 15(4) backward classes.
- Article 16 guarantees equal opportunity in public employment; 16(4) permits reservation for backward classes.
- Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 18 abolishes titles (military/academic exempt).
- Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not 'titles' and do not violate Article 18.

items.title: Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22)
items.body:
## In one line

Articles 19-22 protect personal freedoms — speech, movement, life and personal liberty, and protection when arrested.

## Why it is asked

Article 21's expansion (Maneka Gandhi, Puttaswamy) and preventive-detention rules are exam staples.

## Article 19 — Six Freedoms

Guaranteed to **citizens**, each subject to **reasonable restrictions**:
1. Speech & expression
2. Assemble peaceably **without arms**
3. Form associations/unions
4. Move freely throughout India
5. Reside & settle anywhere in India
6. Practise any profession, occupation, trade or business

(The old seventh freedom — to acquire, hold and dispose of **property** — was deleted by the 44th Amendment.)

## Articles 20-22 — Protections

- **Article 20** — three protections: **no ex-post-facto (retrospective) criminal legislation**, **no double jeopardy**, **no self-incrimination**. Applies to all persons.
- **Article 21** — **life & personal liberty**, deprivable only by **procedure established by law**. **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)** held the procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable**, greatly expanding Art 21 (privacy, clean environment, livelihood, speedy trial).
- **Article 21A** — **Right to Education** for children **6-14 years**, added by the **86th Amendment Act, 2002**.
- **Article 22** — safeguards on ordinary arrest: be informed of the grounds, **consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice**, and be produced before a magistrate within **24 hours (excluding travel time)**. These safeguards do **NOT** apply fully to a person held under a **preventive detention** law, which has its own rules (advisory board review for detention beyond **3 months**).

## Terms explained

- **Reasonable restrictions** — lawful limits the State may place on the six freedoms.
- **‘Procedure established by law’** — liberty can be taken only by a fair legal procedure (Article 21).
- **Preventive detention** — holding a person to stop a feared future act, without a trial.
- **Ex-post-facto law** — a law that punishes an act which was not an offence when it was done; Article 20 forbids this.

## TL;DR

- Article 19 grants six freedoms to citizens, each subject to reasonable restrictions.
- Article 20 gives protection against ex-post-facto laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination.
- Article 21 protects life & personal liberty; Maneka Gandhi (1978) made 'procedure' just, fair and reasonable and expanded its scope.
- Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes education a fundamental right for children aged 6-14.
- Article 22 requires arrested persons be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours and governs preventive detention.

items.title: Against Exploitation & Freedom of Religion (Articles 23-28)
items.body:
## In one line

Articles 23-28 ban forced labour and child labour and guarantee freedom of religion.

## Why it is asked

The child-labour age limit (14) and the four religion articles (25-28) are common anchors.

## Right against Exploitation (23-24)

- **Article 23** — prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour**; applies against **private persons** too. Exception: the State may impose **compulsory service** (for example, military) for public purposes.
- **Article 24** — bars employment of **children below 14** in factories, mines or hazardous work.

## Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28)

| Article | Provision |
|---|---|
| 25 | Freedom of **conscience** and free profession, practice & propagation of religion (citizens & non-citizens); State may regulate & undertake social reform |
| 26 | Freedom to **manage religious affairs** (denominations may own/administer property) |
| 27 | **No tax** for promotion of a particular religion |
| 28 | **No religious instruction** in wholly State-funded institutions |

- India's secularism = **equal respect for all religions**; the State has no official religion.

## Terms explained

- **Begar** — forced labour taken without any payment.
- **Traffic in human beings** — buying, selling or trading people.
- **Propagation** — the freedom to spread or preach one’s religion (Article 25).
- **Secularism** — the State giving equal respect to all religions and having none of its own.

## TL;DR

- Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar and forced labour, even by private persons; compulsory State service is an exception.
- Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
- Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion.
- Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a religion; Article 28 bars religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions.
- Articles 25-28 apply to both citizens and non-citizens.
keyPoints: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar and forced labour, even by private persons; compulsory State service is an exception.
Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion.
Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a religion; Article 28 bars religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions.
Articles 25-28 apply to both citizens and non-citizens.

items.title: Cultural-Educational Rights & Constitutional Remedies (Articles 29-32)
items.body:
## In one line

Articles 29-30 protect minorities' culture and education, and Article 32 lets a citizen go straight to the Supreme Court to enforce a right.

## Why it is asked

Article 32 ('heart and soul' of the Constitution) and the five writs are among the most asked topics.

## Cultural & Educational Rights (29-30)

- **Article 29** — protects the right of any section of citizens to conserve its **distinct language, script or culture**; no denial of admission to State-aided institutions on grounds of religion/race/caste/language.
- **Article 30** — **religious and linguistic minorities** may **establish and administer** educational institutions of their choice (State cannot discriminate in aid).

## Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies

- Ambedkar called it the **'heart and soul' of the Constitution**. It lets a person **move the Supreme Court directly** for enforcement of FRs.
- The SC (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226) can issue **five writs**:

| Writ | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Habeas Corpus** | 'produce the body' — against unlawful detention (even private persons) |
| **Mandamus** | 'we command' — directs a public authority to do its legal duty |
| **Prohibition** | stops a lower court/tribunal exceeding jurisdiction (before) |
| **Certiorari** | quashes a lower court/authority's order (after; also curative) |
| **Quo Warranto** | questions a person's right to hold a public office |

- **High Court writ power (Art 226) is wider** — it covers FRs **and other legal rights**; Art 32 is only for FRs.

## Terms explained

- **Writ** — a formal written order issued by a court.
- **Habeas Corpus** — ‘produce the body’; a writ against unlawful detention.
- **Mandamus** — ‘we command’; a writ ordering a public authority to do its legal duty.
- **Minority** — a religious or linguistic group that is smaller in number within the population.

## TL;DR

- Article 29 protects the distinct language, script and culture of any section of citizens.
- Article 30 lets religious and linguistic minorities establish and administer educational institutions.
- Article 32 is the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' (Ambedkar) — direct access to the Supreme Court for FR enforcement.
- Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
- High Court writ jurisdiction (Art 226) is wider than the Supreme Court's (Art 32) — it covers FRs and other legal rights.

items.title: Articles 33-35 & Exceptions (31A/31B/31C, Ninth Schedule)
items.body:
## In one line

Articles 33-35 and the saving clauses 31A, 31B and 31C set out when Fundamental Rights can be restricted or shielded.

## Why it is asked

The Ninth Schedule, basic-structure review and emergency suspension (Articles 358/359) are frequent traps.

## Articles 33-35

- **Article 33** — Parliament may **restrict/abrogate FRs** for members of the **armed forces, police, paramilitary and intelligence agencies** to ensure discipline.
- **Article 34** — restriction on FRs while **martial law** is in force; Parliament may **indemnify** officers for acts done to restore order. (Martial law is **not defined** in the Constitution.)
- **Article 35** — only **Parliament** (not State legislatures) may make laws to give effect to certain FRs (for example, punishing untouchability, trafficking).

## Saving clauses / exceptions

| Article | Effect |
|---|---|
| **31A** | Saves laws for acquisition of estates etc. from Arts 14 & 19 |
| **31B + Ninth Schedule** | Shields listed laws from FR challenge; but post-**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** laws can be reviewed if they violate the **basic structure** (I.R. Coelho, 2007) |
| **31C** | Saves laws implementing DPSPs 39(b)/(c) from Arts 14 & 19 |

## Suspension in Emergency

- During a **National Emergency (Art 352)**, Article **358** automatically suspends **Article 19**; Article **359** lets the President suspend enforcement of other FRs.
- The **44th Amendment (1978)** provides that **Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended**, even during an emergency.

## Terms explained

- **Martial law** — temporary rule by the military when normal administration breaks down (not defined in the Constitution).
- **Saving clause** — a provision (such as 31A, 31B, 31C) that shields certain laws from being struck down.
- **Ninth Schedule** — the list of laws protected from Fundamental-Rights challenge under Article 31B.
- **National Emergency (Article 352)** — a crisis declaration during which some rights can be suspended.

## TL;DR

- Article 33 lets Parliament restrict FRs of armed/police/paramilitary forces; Article 34 covers martial law and indemnity.
- Article 35 reserves to Parliament alone the power to make laws enforcing certain FRs.
- 31B and the Ninth Schedule shield laws from FR challenge, but post-1973 laws are reviewable against the basic structure (I.R. Coelho, 2007).
- Article 358 auto-suspends Article 19 during a National Emergency; Article 359 suspends enforcement of other FRs.
- The 44th Amendment 1978 makes Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even in an emergency.

items.title: Articles 12–22 Clause by Clause — Equality and Freedom in Detail
items.body:
## Articles 12 to 22, clause by clause

**In one line:** each Article from 12 to 22 has sub-clauses and amendments that examiners turn into statement questions — who counts as "State", which clause allows which reservation, which grounds limit free speech, and what protection an arrested person gets.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC and APPSC test 13(3), 15(4)/(5)/(6), 16(4A), 19(2), 20(3), 21's expansion and 22's preventive-detention rules almost every year.

**The story**

### What a right is
- **Rights** are **claims** of citizens against the State (UPSC 2017); one implication of **equality** is the absence of **privileges** (UPSC 2017); the **Rule of Law** means limitation of powers, equality before law, and liberty and civil rights (UPSC 2018).
- Fundamental Rights are justiciable but not absolute — reasonable restrictions may be imposed; Part III is popularly called the Magna Carta of India.

### Article 12 — "State"
- Includes the **Government and Parliament of India**, the **government and legislature of each state**, all **local authorities** (municipalities, panchayats) and **other authorities** created by the Constitution or law, under government control — so that every body exercising **public functions** is accountable for Fundamental Rights.

### Article 13 — laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
| Clause | Rule |
|---|---|
| **13(1)** | **Pre-constitutional laws** are void to the extent they are inconsistent with FRs |
| **13(2)** | The State shall not make a law that **takes away or abridges** FRs; such a law is void to that extent |
| **13(3)** | "**Law**" includes an **ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation, notification** and custom having the force of law |
- Article 13 makes the courts guardians of FRs (**judicial review**). Article **368** is the separate power to **amend** the Constitution. Whether an amendment is "law" under 13(2) was the fight in **Shankari Prasad (1951)** (no), **Golaknath (1967)** (yes) and **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** (no, but the basic structure binds).

### Article 14 — equality before law
- Combines **equality before law** (British) and **equal protection of the laws** (American); applies to all persons. A law conferring unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power on the executive violates Article 14 (UPSC 2021).

### Article 15 — no discrimination, with special-provision clauses
- Bars discrimination against **citizens** on **religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth** — including access to shops, hotels, wells and public places.
- **15(3)** – special provisions for **women and children**. **15(4)** – for **socially and educationally backward classes** and SC/ST (added by the **1st Amendment, 1951** after **Champakam Dorairajan**). **15(5)** – reservation in **educational institutions, including private ones** (except minority institutions) — **93rd Amendment, 2005**. **15(6)** – up to **10%** for **economically weaker sections (EWS)** — **103rd Amendment, 2019**.

### Article 16 — equality in public employment
| Clause | Content |
|---|---|
| **16(3)** | **Parliament** may prescribe **residence** as a condition for certain jobs |
| **16(4)** | Reservation for **backward classes not adequately represented** |
| **16(4A)** | Reservation in **promotion** for SC/ST (**77th Amendment, 1995**); consequential seniority (85th, 2001) |
| **16(4B)** | **Carry-forward** of unfilled reserved vacancies beyond the 50% limit (**81st Amendment, 2000**) |
| **16(5)** | Office of a **religious institution** may be kept for persons of that religion |
| **16(6)** | **10% EWS** reservation in posts (**103rd Amendment, 2019**) |
- **Indra Sawhney (1992)** (the Mandal case) upheld **27% OBC** reservation but set a **50% ceiling**, excluded the **creamy layer**, barred reservation in **promotions** (later restored for SC/ST by 16(4A)) and held that **caste** can identify backward classes.

### Articles 17 and 18
- **17** abolishes **untouchability**; it is punishable under the **Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955**, renamed the **Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976**. The word "untouchability" is **not defined** in the Constitution.
- **18** abolishes **titles** except **military and academic** distinctions; no citizen may accept a foreign title without the **President's** consent. In **Balaji Raghavan (1996)** the Court held **Bharat Ratna / Padma** awards are **not titles**.

### Article 19 — six freedoms of citizens and their limits
- Six freedoms (originally seven — **19(1)(f) property** was deleted by the **44th Amendment**): **speech and expression**, **assembly** (peacefully, without arms), **association** (including **co-operative societies**, added by the 97th Amendment), **movement**, **residence**, **profession**.
- **Freedom of the press** is not named but is part of **speech and expression** (**Romesh Thappar, 1950**).
- Reasonable restrictions under **19(2)**: **sovereignty and integrity of India**, **security of the State**, **friendly relations with foreign States**, **public order**, **decency or morality**, **contempt of court**, **defamation** and **incitement to an offence**. The **1st Amendment (1951)** added public order, friendly relations and incitement; the **16th Amendment (1963)** added **sovereignty and integrity**.

### Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction (all persons; cannot be suspended in an Emergency)
| Clause | Protection |
|---|---|
| **20(1)** | No **ex-post-facto** criminal law — no conviction for an act that was not an offence when done |
| **20(2)** | No **double jeopardy** — no prosecution and punishment twice for the same offence |
| **20(3)** | No **self-incrimination** — an accused cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself |

### Article 21 — life and personal liberty
- **A.K. Gopalan (1950)** read "procedure established by law" narrowly; **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** held the procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable** — bringing in the American **due process** idea.
- Rights read into Article 21 include: **privacy** (Puttaswamy 2017), **livelihood** (Olga Tellis 1985), **speedy trial** (Hussainara Khatoon 1979), **clean environment**, **health**, **shelter**, **dignity of prisoners** (Sunil Batra 1978), **travel abroad** (Maneka Gandhi), **marry a person of one's choice**, and **die with dignity** (Common Cause 2018).
- **Article 21A** — free and compulsory **education** for children of **6–14** years (**86th Amendment, 2002**); the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009** gives it effect.

### Article 22 — arrest and detention
- **Ordinary arrest:** right to be **informed of the grounds**, to **consult a lawyer** of choice, to be **produced before a magistrate within 24 hours** (excluding travel time), and to be **released** unless the magistrate orders further detention. These do **not** apply to an **enemy alien** or a person held under **preventive detention**.
- **Preventive detention:** detention beyond **three months** needs an **Advisory Board** report (judges of a High Court); the grounds must be communicated and the detenu may **represent** against the order. Laws include the **Preventive Detention Act 1950**, **MISA 1971**, **COFEPOSA 1974** and the **National Security Act 1980**.

## Don't confuse
- **15(5) = education (93rd)**; **16(4A) = promotion (77th)**; **16(4B) = carry-forward (81st)**; **15(6)/16(6) = EWS (103rd)**.
- **Gopalan = narrow "procedure"; Maneka = just, fair and reasonable.**
- Article **20(3)** (self-incrimination) is about **witness against oneself**, not about arrest.

**TL;DR**
- 13(3) "law" includes ordinances, by-laws, rules, notifications.
- 15(3) women/children; 15(4) backward classes (1st Amdt); 15(5) education (93rd); 15(6) EWS (103rd).
- 16(3) residence by Parliament; 16(4A) promotion (77th); 16(4B) carry-forward (81st); Indra Sawhney: 50% cap, creamy layer.
- 17: PCR Act 1955/1976; 18: titles abolished, awards not titles (Balaji Raghavan).
- 19(2) eight grounds; 1st and 16th Amendments; press freedom (Romesh Thappar).
- 21: Gopalan → Maneka; privacy, livelihood, speedy trial, die with dignity; 21A (86th, RTE Act 2009); 22: 24 hours, Advisory Board after three months.
keyPoints: Article 13(3): 'law' includes an ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation and notification; 13(1) voids inconsistent pre-constitutional laws.
Article 15(4) came by the 1st Amendment (1951) after Champakam Dorairajan; 15(5) (93rd, 2005) covers private educational institutions; 15(6) and 16(6) (103rd, 2019) give 10% EWS reservation.
16(3) lets Parliament prescribe residence; 16(4A) promotion reservation (77th, 1995); 16(4B) carry-forward (81st, 2000); Indra Sawhney (1992): 27% OBC, 50% ceiling, creamy layer.
Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976; Balaji Raghavan (1996): Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles.

Article 19(2) grounds include sovereignty and integrity (16th Amendment 1963), public order, friendly relations, decency, contempt of court, defamation and incitement; press freedom is part of 19(1)(a) (Romesh Thappar).
Article 21 includes privacy, livelihood (Olga Tellis), speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon), prisoners' dignity (Sunil Batra) and die with dignity (Common Cause 2018).
Article 22 safeguards do not apply to enemy aliens or preventive detainees; detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board; NSA 1980, COFEPOSA 1974, MISA 1971.

items.title: Articles 23–35 in Detail — Exploitation, Religion, Minorities, Remedies & Exceptions
items.body:
## Articles 23 to 35, and the saving clauses

**In one line:** Articles 23–30 protect against exploitation and protect religion and minorities; Article 32 is the remedy; Articles 33–35 and 31A–31C are the exceptions.

**Why it is asked:** writ limits (against whom a writ lies), the four kinds of institutions under Article 28, and martial law vs Emergency are frequent statement questions.

**The story**

### Right against Exploitation
- **Article 23** bans **traffic in human beings**, **begar** and **forced labour**; it protects against **private persons** too, and **economic compulsion** (paying less than minimum wage) is also forced labour. **Exception:** the State may impose **compulsory service** for public purposes, such as **military** service.
- **Article 24** bars **children below 14** from **factories, mines** and **hazardous** work; **harmless** work is not barred. The **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005** created national and state child-rights commissions.

### Right to Freedom of Religion
- **Article 25** — freedom of **conscience** and the right to **profess, practise and propagate** religion, for **citizens and non-citizens**. **Forced conversion** is not covered. The State may **regulate** secular activities and undertake **social reform**. Wearing and carrying a **kirpan** is part of the Sikh religion; "Hindus" here includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists**.
- **Article 26** — every **religious denomination** may set up institutions, manage its own religious affairs, and **own and administer property**. A denomination = a group with **common beliefs**, a **common organisation** and a **distinct name**.
- **Article 27** — no person can be compelled to pay **taxes** for promoting a particular religion (a **fee** for services is allowed).
- **Article 28** — four kinds of institutions:

| Institution | Religious instruction? |
|---|---|
| **Wholly maintained by the State** | **Completely prohibited** |
| Administered by the State but **established under a trust** | **Permitted** |
| **Recognised** by the State | Permitted on a **voluntary** basis |
| Receiving **aid** from the State | Permitted on a **voluntary** basis |

### Cultural and Educational Rights
- **Article 29** — any section of citizens with a distinct **language, script or culture** may conserve it; admission to State-run or aided institutions cannot be denied on **religion, race, caste or language**. It protects **religious and linguistic minorities** and, the Court has held, the **majority** too.
- **Article 30** — only **minorities (religious and linguistic)** may **establish and administer** educational institutions of their choice; the State cannot discriminate in **aid**. **Compensation** must be fixed if a minority institution's property is acquired.

### Article 31 and the saving clauses
- **Article 31** (right to property) was **omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978)**.

| Article | What it saves |
|---|---|
| **31A** | Five kinds of laws from challenge under **Articles 14 and 19**: **acquisition of estates**; State **taking over management** of property; **amalgamation of corporations**; changing rights of **directors or shareholders**; ending or changing **mining leases** |
| **31B** | Acts in the **Ninth Schedule** from FR challenge; but laws added after **24 April 1973** can be tested on the **basic structure** (Coelho 2007) |
| **31C** | Laws giving effect to **Article 39(b) and 39(c)** from challenge under **Articles 14 and 19**. Its second part (barring courts from asking whether a law really gives effect to the policy) was **struck down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**; the **42nd Amendment's** extension of 31C to **all** Directive Principles was struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)** |

### Article 32 — the remedy
- The **most important** safeguard: a person can move the **Supreme Court directly**; Article 32 can be used **only for violation of Fundamental Rights**. Ambedkar called it the "**heart and soul**" of the Constitution.
- **Parliament** may empower **other courts** to issue writs (Article 32(3)). Enforcement can be **suspended** during a National Emergency under **Article 359**.
- **Before 1950**, only the High Courts of **Bombay, Madras and Calcutta** could issue writs.
- The Supreme Court's writ power is **narrower** in scope than a High Court's (only FRs) but **wider in territory** (all of India).

| Writ | Lies against | Does NOT lie |
|---|---|---|
| **Habeas Corpus** | **Public authorities and private individuals** | Where detention is **lawful**; for **contempt** of a legislature or court; by a competent court's order; outside the court's jurisdiction |
| **Mandamus** | Public officials, public bodies, **inferior courts**, tribunals, government | **Private** individuals or bodies; **discretionary** duties; **contractual** obligations; the **President**, **Governors**; the **Chief Justice of a High Court** acting judicially |
| **Prohibition** | Only **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies | **Administrative** or **legislative** bodies, private persons |
| **Certiorari** | Judicial, quasi-judicial and also **administrative** authorities affecting rights — both **preventive and curative** | Legislative bodies, private persons |
| **Quo Warranto** | A **substantive public office** created by statute or the Constitution | **Ministerial** or **private** offices; **any interested person** may apply (not only the aggrieved) |

### Articles 33, 34 and 35
- **33** — **Parliament** may restrict or abrogate the FRs of the **armed forces, paramilitary, police, intelligence** and analogous forces, for **discipline**.
- **34** — restrictions while **martial law** is in force in an area; Parliament may **indemnify** officers for acts done to restore order. **Martial law** is **not defined** in the Constitution.
- **35** — **Parliament alone** (not state legislatures) makes laws on: **residence** for jobs (16(3)); empowering **other courts** to issue writs (32(3)); restricting FRs of forces (33); **indemnity** under martial law (34); **punishing untouchability** (17) and **trafficking / forced labour** (23).

| Point | Martial law | National Emergency |
|---|---|---|
| Affects | Only **Fundamental Rights** | FRs, **Centre–state relations**, revenue, Parliament's term |
| Courts and government | **Suspends** government and ordinary courts | They **continue** |
| Ground | To **restore law and order** broken down for any reason | **War, external aggression or armed rebellion** |
| Area | **Specific areas** | Whole country or any part |
| Provision | **No specific provision** | **Specific and detailed** provision (Article 352) |

### Significance and criticism (source text)
- **Significance:** basis of **political democracy**; material and moral protection; safeguard of **individual liberty**; help the **rule of law**; protect **minorities**; strengthen the **secular** State; check the **absolute power** of the government.
- **Criticism:** **excessive limitations**; **no socio-economic rights** (such as the right to work); **lack of clarity**; **no permanency** (Parliament can amend them); **suspension during Emergency**; **expensive remedy**; **preventive detention**; **no consistent philosophy**.

## Don't confuse
- **Habeas Corpus lies even against private persons; Mandamus does not.**
- **Prohibition only for judicial bodies; Certiorari also for administrative bodies.**
- **Article 29 = any section of citizens; Article 30 = minorities only.**

**TL;DR**
- 23: trafficking, begar; also private persons; military service allowed. 24: below 14; CPCR Act 2005.
- 25: citizens and non-citizens; kirpan; Hindus include Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists. 26: denomination. 27: no tax. 28: four institution types.
- 31A five laws; 31B Ninth Schedule (post-24 April 1973 reviewable); 31C — 39(b)/(c); second part struck in Kesavananda.
- 32: only FRs; pre-1950 writs only Bombay, Madras, Calcutta HCs; writ limits table.
- 33 forces; 34 martial law (undefined); 35 Parliament alone; martial law vs Emergency table.
keyPoints: Article 23 binds private persons too and treats economic compulsion as forced labour; compulsory military service is the exception; Article 24 allows harmless work by children.
Under Article 25 the kirpan is part of Sikh religion and 'Hindus' include Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists; Article 26 denominations may own and administer property.
Article 28: no religious instruction in wholly State-maintained institutions; permitted in State-administered trust institutions; voluntary in recognised or aided ones.
Article 31A saves five kinds of laws (estates, management, amalgamation, directors/shareholders, mining leases) from Articles 14 and 19.
Article 31C's second part was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati; its extension to all DPSPs by the 42nd Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills.
Before 1950 only the Bombay, Madras and Calcutta High Courts issued writs; Parliament may empower other courts (Article 32(3)).

Habeas Corpus lies against private persons; Mandamus not against private bodies, the President or Governors; Prohibition only against judicial/quasi-judicial bodies; Quo Warranto — any interested person, substantive public office.
Martial law is not defined in the Constitution, affects only FRs and suspends ordinary courts; Article 35 gives Parliament alone power over 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34, 17 and 23 laws.

items.title: Landmark Fundamental-Rights Cases — From Gopalan to Puttaswamy
items.body:
## The cases that shaped Part III

**In one line:** the Supreme Court has widened, defended and sometimes restricted Fundamental Rights through a chain of judgments; each case is asked as a name–holding pair.

**Why it is asked:** "Which case held privacy a Fundamental Right?", "Which case started PIL?", "Which case set the 50% cap?" — these match questions appear in every polity paper.

**The story**

### Personal liberty and fair procedure
| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras** | **1950** | Detention under the **Preventive Detention Act** valid if it follows a law made by the legislature; **Article 22 self-contained**; **procedure established by law** preferred over **due process** |
| **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India** | **1978** | **Right to travel abroad** is part of Article 21 (Passport Act case); the procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable** |
| **ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla** (Habeas Corpus case) | **1976** | During the Emergency detenus **could not file habeas corpus** under Article 226; **Justice H.R. Khanna dissented**; **overruled in Puttaswamy (2017)** |
| **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India** | **2017** | **Privacy** is a Fundamental Right under **Article 21** (nine-judge bench) |
| **Common Cause v. Union of India** | **2018** | **Right to die with dignity**; **passive euthanasia** and **living wills** recognised |

### Amending Fundamental Rights
| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Shankari Prasad** | **1951** | Upheld the **1st Amendment**; Parliament can amend FRs — an amendment is **not "law"** under Article 13(2) |
| **I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab** | **1967** | An amendment **is "law"**; Parliament **cannot abridge FRs** (narrow majority) |
| **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala** | **1973** | **13-judge bench**; overruled Golaknath; Parliament can amend any part but **not the basic structure** |
| **Minerva Mills v. Union of India** | **1980** | Struck down clauses **(4) and (5) of Article 368** (42nd Amendment); **judicial review** and the **balance between FRs and DPSPs** are basic structure |
| **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu** | **2007** | **Ninth Schedule** laws added after **24 April 1973** are open to review |

### PIL and social justice
| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Mumbai Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai** | **1976** | **Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer** laid the foundation of **PIL** — technicalities must not block justice |
| **Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration** | **1978** | **Prisoners** keep their Article 21 rights; prison reforms |
| **Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar** | **1979** | **Speedy trial** is part of Article 21 (undertrial prisoners) |
| **Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India** | **1984** | Release and rehabilitation of **bonded labourers**; anyone acting in good faith can file a PIL |
| **Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation** | **1985** | **Right to livelihood** is part of the right to life (pavement dwellers) |
| **M.C. Mehta v. Union of India** | **1986** | **Absolute liability** (replacing strict liability) for **hazardous industries** (Oleum gas leak) |
| **Indra Sawhney v. Union of India** (Mandal case) | **1992** | Upheld **27% OBC** quota; **50% ceiling**; **creamy layer** excluded; no reservation in **promotions** or some high posts |
| **Unnikrishnan v. State of A.P.** | **1993** | Education up to **14 years** is a Fundamental Right under Article 21 — led to **Article 21A** |
| **Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India** | **2022** | Upheld the **103rd Amendment** (**10% EWS** quota) by 3:2 |

### Expression, equality and gender justice
| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras** | **1950** | **Freedom of the press** is part of freedom of speech and expression |
| **State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan** | **1951** | Struck down caste-based (communal) admission quotas → **1st Amendment** added **Article 15(4)** |
| **Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan** | **1997** | **Vishaka Guidelines** against **sexual harassment at the workplace** |
| **NALSA v. Union of India** | **2014** | Transgender persons recognised as the **third gender** (Articles 14, 19, 21) |
| **Shreya Singhal v. Union of India** | **2015** | Struck down **Section 66A** of the **IT Act** (online speech) |
| **Shayara Bano v. Union of India** | **2017** | **Instant triple talaq** unconstitutional — arbitrary, violates **Article 14** |
| **Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India** | **2018** | Decriminalised consensual same-sex relations (**Section 377** IPC read down) |
| **Joseph Shine v. Union of India** | **2018** | Struck down **Section 497** IPC (**adultery**) — violated Articles **14, 15 and 21** |
| **Indian Young Lawyers Association** (Sabarimala) | **2018** | Women of **all ages** may enter **Sabarimala** temple |
| **Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala** | **1986** | Students who stood respectfully but did not **sing the national anthem** could not be expelled (Article 25) |

### Andhra Pradesh angle
- The **High Court of Andhra Pradesh** at **Amaravati** began functioning separately on **1 January 2019**, after bifurcation from the common High Court at Hyderabad; its writ power under **Article 226** is wider than the Supreme Court's under Article 32.
- **Unnikrishnan (1993)** — the education case that led to Article 21A — arose from **Andhra Pradesh** (Unnikrishnan v. State of A.P.).

## Don't confuse
- **Gopalan (1950) narrow; Maneka (1978) wide.** **ADM Jabalpur (1976) overruled by Puttaswamy (2017).**
- **Golaknath (1967) — Parliament cannot amend FRs; Kesavananda (1973) — it can, except the basic structure.**
- **Olga Tellis = livelihood; Hussainara = speedy trial; Sunil Batra = prisoners; Bandhua Mukti Morcha = bonded labour.**

**TL;DR**
- Liberty: Gopalan 1950 → Maneka 1978; ADM Jabalpur 1976 (Khanna dissent); Puttaswamy 2017 privacy; Common Cause 2018 dignity in death.
- Amendment: Shankari 1951 → Golaknath 1967 → Kesavananda 1973 → Minerva 1980 → Coelho 2007.
- PIL: Mumbai Kamgar Sabha 1976 (Krishna Iyer); Bandhua Mukti Morcha 1984; M.C. Mehta 1986 absolute liability.
- Equality: Champakam 1951 → 15(4); Indra Sawhney 1992; Janhit Abhiyan 2022 (EWS).
- Gender/expression: Romesh Thappar, Vishaka, NALSA, Shreya Singhal, Shayara Bano, Navtej, Joseph Shine, Sabarimala.
keyPoints: A.K. Gopalan (1950) treated Article 22 as self-contained and preferred procedure established by law; Maneka Gandhi (1978) added the right to travel abroad and a just, fair and reasonable procedure.
ADM Jabalpur (1976) denied habeas corpus during the Emergency; Justice H.R. Khanna dissented; overruled by Puttaswamy (2017).
Shankari Prasad (1951) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges) vs Golaknath (1967); Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368(4) and (5).
Mumbai Kamgar Sabha (1976, Krishna Iyer) founded PIL; Hussainara Khatoon (1979) speedy trial; Olga Tellis (1985) livelihood; M.C. Mehta (1986) absolute liability.
Unnikrishnan v. State of A.P. (1993) made education up to 14 a right; Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld 10% EWS quota.
Romesh Thappar (1950) press freedom; Champakam Dorairajan (1951) led to Article 15(4); Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A IT Act.
NALSA (2014) third gender; Shayara Bano (2017) triple talaq; Navtej Johar (2018) Section 377; Joseph Shine (2018) adultery; Sabarimala (2018); Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) anthem.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court at Amaravati functions separately from 1 January 2019.

items.title: For Mains — Fundamental Rights
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance; clauses M3-1, M3-15a)

Fundamental Rights questions reward **judicial-evolution narrative + the FR-DPSP balance + contemporary rights debates**, not article-listing.

| Dimension | What to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Significance** | Magna Carta of India; limits on State; political democracy; Art 32 the 'heart and soul' (Ambedkar) |
| **Judicial expansion** | A.K. Gopalan (1950) → Maneka Gandhi (1978, golden triangle 14-19-21) → Art 21 as reservoir of rights |
| **FR vs DPSP** | Champakam Dorairajan (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973, basic structure) → Minerva Mills (1980, balance/harmony) |
| **Contemporary rights** | Privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), Sec 377 decriminalised (Navtej Johar 2018), Sabarimala (2018), live-in/choice in marriage, euthanasia (Common Cause 2018) |
| **Criticism / limits** | Preventive detention (Art 22), reasonable restrictions, Ninth Schedule abuse, cost of litigation, no explicit socio-economic rights |
| **Way forward** | PIL and legal aid, locus-standi dilution, balance activism with restraint |

**Data / authorities to quote:** Maneka Gandhi (1978); K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, 9-judge, privacy under Art 21); Navtej Singh Johar (2018); I.R. Coelho (2007, Ninth Schedule reviewable against basic structure); Olga Tellis (livelihood); Hussainara Khatoon (speedy trial); 44th Amendment (1978) shielding Arts 20-21; RTE Act 2009 operationalising Art 21A.

**AP angle:** Article 21A / RTE is a live governance test in AP (enrolment, pupil-teacher norms, Amma Vodi-type schemes supporting the right to education); Art 23 and bonded-labour abolition remain relevant to AP's agrarian and brick-kiln labour contexts. Reservation debates (Arts 15(4)/16(4)) connect to AP's own BC/SC/ST and 10% EWS implementation.

**Use in answers:** anchor with Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' line for Art 32; use the Gopalan→Maneka→Puttaswamy arc as a crisp timeline; for FR-DPSP, use the four-case ladder ending at Minerva Mills' 'harmony and balance'; close with the activism-vs-restraint caution. A golden-triangle (Art 14-19-21) diagram earns structure marks.
keyPoints: Lead with Art 32 ('heart and soul') and the Gopalan → Maneka → Puttaswamy judicial-expansion arc.
Explain the FR-DPSP conflict via Champakam → Golaknath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills (harmony/balance).
Cite contemporary rights: privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), Navtej Johar (2018), euthanasia (Common Cause 2018).
Note limits: preventive detention, reasonable restrictions, Ninth Schedule reviewable post-I.R. Coelho (2007).
AP angle: RTE/Art 21A governance, Art 23 bonded labour, reservation (15(4)/16(4)) and EWS implementation.
Close by balancing judicial activism with restraint; use the golden-triangle (14-19-21) framing.
